chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Momentum and Trend Following Actually Are

lessons.title: What Is Momentum? The Market Anomaly That Shouldn't Exist

children.text: In January 2023, Suzlon Energy traded at a little over eight rupees a share, a stock most brokers had written off after a decade of debt trouble and repeated shareholder dilution. By July 2024, the same stock had crossed eighty rupees, roughly a tenfold move in eighteen months. Nothing about the company changed overnight. What changed was that the stock had already started moving, and once it did, it kept moving, pulling in more buyers, more volume, and more attention with every new high. An investor who bought Suzlon in early 2023, not because it looked cheap on any fundamental measure but simply because it had already gone up and kept climbing, would have been trading on momentum. This lesson is about why that approach works, and why, according to decades of finance theory, it should not.

body.text: Momentum is the tendency for securities that have performed well over the recent past to keep performing well in the near future, and for securities that have performed poorly to keep performing poorly. It means buying strength and selling weakness, the opposite of the classic instinct to buy low and sell high.

children.text: The Efficient Market Problem: Why Momentum Shouldn't Exist

markDefs.definition: The theory that a security's price already reflects all publicly available information, so future price changes should be unpredictable from past prices alone.

children.text: , the dominant framework taught in most finance courses, says a stock's price already reflects all publicly available information. If that were fully true, past price movement would carry no information about future price movement. A stock that rose ten percent last month should be no more likely to rise next month than a stock that fell ten percent, because whatever caused last month's move is already priced in. Momentum flatly contradicts this. Stocks that have gone up tend to keep going up, on average, for a period of roughly three to twelve months, before eventually reversing. This is not a fringe finding confined to one market or one decade. It has been documented across US equities, European equities, Japanese equities, commodities, currencies, and Indian equities. An anomaly this persistent and this widely replicated is one of the more uncomfortable facts for a theory that says prices should already know everything.
Defining Momentum: Buying Strength, Not Value

Momentum sits philosophically opposite to value investing. A value investor buys a stock because they believe the market has priced it too low relative to its underlying worth, and waits for the price to catch up. A momentum trader does not ask whether a stock is cheap or expensive at all. They ask only whether the stock's recent price trend is strong enough to be likely to continue, and they are willing to buy a stock that already looks expensive by every traditional measure, as long as the trend supports it. The two philosophies can, and often do, produce opposite positions in the same stock at the same time. A value investor may be selling a stock precisely because it has run up too far. A momentum trader may be buying it for exactly the same reason.
How Momentum Is Measured: Formation and Holding Periods

markDefs.definition: The look-back window used to rank securities by their past return before forming a momentum portfolio, typically three to twelve months.
The length of time a momentum position is held before the portfolio is re-ranked and rebalanced, typically one to twelve months.

children.text: Momentum strategies are built around two windows. The
is the look-back window used to rank stocks by past return. The

is how long the resulting position is held before being re-evaluated. A common convention, used in the original academic momentum research, is a twelve-month formation period that excludes the most recent month, followed by a three-month holding period. The exclusion of the most recent month exists because stocks often show short-term reversal in the first few weeks after a sharp move, and including that month would contaminate a pure momentum signal with short-term noise that has nothing to do with the underlying trend.

body.text: Notice the gap between winners and losers does not close, it widens, for most of the holding period shown here. This gradual, sustained separation, not a one-time jump on day one, is the signature of a real momentum effect as opposed to random noise.

children.text: Case Study: Reading a Momentum Run on the NSE

Go back to Suzlon Energy. Through 2023 and into 2024, the stock moved through several distinct phases that a momentum trader tracks: a base after years of decline, an initial breakout on improved order inflow and debt reduction, a sustained uptrend as more traders and funds noticed the move and piled in, and eventually a period of sharp, choppy swings as the stock became crowded with short-term speculative volume, much of it through NSE derivatives. None of this requires predicting Suzlon's fundamentals months in advance. A momentum trader is not trying to value the company. They are trying to identify that a trend is underway and stay in it for as long as the trend has statistical evidence of continuing, then get out before it reverses.

body.caption: Suzlon Energy: an illustrative momentum run (rounded, illustrative figures, not exact historical data)

body.text: A momentum run like this does not end gently. Stocks that have moved this far, this fast, are also the ones most exposed to a sharp, sudden reversal once the trend breaks, sometimes called a momentum crash. Position sizing and exit discipline for exactly this situation are covered later in this course.

body.title: Momentum or something else?
body.question: An investor screens NSE stocks for those trading within 5% of their 52-week high, ranks them by their trailing 6-month return, and buys the strongest performers without checking any valuation ratio. What is this investor doing?
options: Value investing, since a 52-week high signals a fundamentally strong company
Momentum investing, buying strength based on recent price performance regardless of valuation
Arbitrage, since two related prices are being compared
Dividend investing, since stocks near their highs tend to pay higher dividends
body.explanation: This is a textbook momentum screen: ranking purely by recent price strength, with no reference to valuation. Value investing, arbitrage, and dividend investing all rest on different criteria entirely.

body.title: Is your friend's instinct backed by the evidence?
body.scenario: A friend tells you: "Whenever a stock is up 80% in a year, I sell any I'm holding, because it's due for a fall."
body.prompt: Does the historical momentum evidence support this instinct? What is it missing?
body.modelAnswer: Not over the typical momentum horizon. The evidence shows that stocks with strong recent performance tend to keep outperforming, on average, over the following 3 to 12 months, before any reversal tends to show up. Selling purely because a stock is up a lot ignores this documented continuation and can mean exiting a trend early, purely on the belief that a large move must reverse soon. That said, the instinct is not baseless over a longer horizon: momentum does eventually fade and can reverse sharply, which is why momentum strategies use a defined holding period and exit rules rather than holding forever on the assumption that a trend never ends.

Indifferent to whether a stock looks cheap or expensive

Main risk: sharp reversal once the trend breaks

columns.label: Value Investing
points: Ranks stocks by price relative to estimated underlying worth
Actively seeks stocks that look cheap on fundamental measures

points: Momentum is the tendency for recent winners to keep winning and recent losers to keep losing, typically over a 3 to 12 month horizon, before eventually reversing.
It directly contradicts a strict reading of the efficient market hypothesis, which is why it is considered one of the most persistent anomalies in finance.
Momentum sits philosophically opposite to value investing: it buys strength regardless of valuation, rather than buying cheap and waiting for the price to catch up.
Momentum strategies are built around a formation period, used to rank securities by past return, and a holding period, for how long the resulting position is held.
The effect has been documented across more than 40 countries and multiple asset classes, and in data going back to at least the 1930s in some studies.
Momentum runs like Suzlon Energy's 2023-2024 rally show the pattern in practice, but strong trends are also the ones most exposed to a sharp reversal once they break.
